newsitem.title: POLAND: High Polish rates no threat to growth -c.banker.
newsitem.headline: High Polish rates no threat to growth -c.banker.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland believes its policy of gradual monetary tightening aimed at meeting 1997 inflation targets should not hamper the country's healthy growth, the bank's deputy president said on Tuesday.
"Given the present level of interest rates, I do not feel any threat for growth from high market rates," Witold Kozinski told Reuters in an interview.

Kozinski said the bank, which last Friday decided to raise from next month obligatory reserves on zloty term deposits and all foreign currency deposits to further tighten monetary policy and defend its 1997 money supply growth target.

"The growth of credit has stabilised, but it has stabilised at a high rate of 2-2.5 billion zlotys per month, which is too much if we want to meet the 28 billion zloty money supply growth for the whole year," he said.
The bank chose the reserve rise, which followed a February increase in mandatory reserve requirement for call deposits, as the most effective way of controlling money supply.
"We chose an instrument which not so much raised the cost of money as reduced its amount in the system," Kozinski said.

The NBP expected the higher costs of funds would eventually force banks to raise credit rates, but even if they chose to cut deposit rates instead, falling inflation should make bank deposits attractive enough to prevent a drop in savings. He reiterated that the bank's prime concern this year was to prevent a further widening of the trade gap.
"Limiting the zloty, high interest rates and higher reserves aim at the ultimate monetary policy target of stabilising the trade balance," Kozinski said.
The trade gap balooned to $3 billion and current account gap to $1.5 billion, respectively, in the first quarter, according to preliminary central bank data.
Some analysts are concerned that high real interest rates, now at about 5.5 percent, could seriously harm growth, which the government has targetted at 5.5 percent this year.

But Kozinski said that, because monetary tightening was gradual and spread over a longer period, the bank was giving enterprises enough time to adjust to more restrictive policy and avoid a slow-down.

"Our actions should cool demand while leaving the supply side relatively unaffected and so firms need time to adjust, cut costs, finance growth more internally...and that is why this process is gradual and the policy is growing more restrictive and will finally bear fruit," he said.
Kozinski said that, because of high liquidity of the banking system and low use of credit by enterprises, the Polish economy remained relatively insensitive to interest rate movements.

"At the end of 1996, interest on credits accounted for three percent of enterprises' costs, while wages accounted for about 20 percent of costs, so they are more sensitive to income policy than monetary policy," he said.
He saw no threat that a further fall in inflation, seen by some analysts at 14.5 percent at the mid-year, and steady official rates, now 22 and 25 percent, would bring the economy to a halt.
Kozinski said growth remained robust, even though real rates grew in the past six months as year-on year inflation fell to 16.6 percent in March from 19.5 percent in October.
Some estimates put GDP growth in the first three months of this year at more than seven percent.
